Warm air rose from below.  
The labyrinth was calling.  
Chapter Thirty-Two  
The Moment We Gave In  
As the guests stumbled into the basement, crying, begging, scrambling in the dark…  
…the hunger inside us finally won.  
It wasn't anger.  
It wasn't cruelty.  
It wasn't even desire.  
It was instinct.  
The same instinct that had consumed the stuffed ones before us. The same instinct that would consume the ones after.  
We weren't human anymore.  
We weren't victims.  
We weren't even ourselves.  
We were part of the ritual.  
We were the hunters.  
And the guests?  
They were the next filling.  
Chapter Thirty-Three  
The Cycle Continues  
I sit on my shelf now, waiting.  
The cabin is quiet.  
The new stuffed ones—fresh from the labyrinth, still warm, still confused—stare back at me with button eyes that haven't yet learned to hunger.  
They will.  
They always do.  
Above us, I hear footsteps.  
Car doors.  
Laughter.  
More guests.  
More company.  
The warmth inside my seams pulses in anticipation.  
I don't fight it anymore.  
I don't want to.  
This is what I am now.  
This is what we are.  
The stuffed ones.  
The keepers of the cabin.  
The hunters in the dark.  
And we are so very hungry.

works.title: WrymWretch
works.blurb: Six elves bond with six dragons as memory itself is erased across the world of Wyrmreach.

passages.heading: WrymWretch
passages.text:
WrymWretch

Story plot line  
ACT I — READER‑READY NARRATIVE

The first sign came quietly, the way rot always does—soft, almost apologetic, as if asking permission to exist. Thalen of Cedarheart noticed it while tracking a silver‑antlered stag through the western groves. The forest should have been humming with life, but the air felt thin, as though something had taken a long breath and forgotten to exhale.

He found the tree at the edge of a clearing. Its trunk had split open from within, not by lightning or age, but by something that pulsed like a second heartbeat. Black ichor seeped from the wound, thick and slow, and when it touched the moss, the moss turned gray and brittle, collapsing into dust that didn’t even remember how to be soil.

passages.heading: WrymWretch
passages.text:
Thalen reached out. The tree recoiled—not in movement, but in spirit. A shiver ran through him, a sensation like brushing against a memory that wasn’t his. He stumbled back, heart pounding, and for a moment he thought he heard a whisper beneath the bark, a voice trying to form a name it no longer possessed.

He ran. Branches clawed at him as he sprinted toward the outpost, and the forest seemed to lean away from him, as if ashamed of what it had shown. By the time he burst through the wooden gates, he could barely speak.

“The forest is… forgetting,” he managed. “Something is making it forget.”

The rangers exchanged uneasy glances. They had heard rumors. None dared speak the name behind them.

Not yet.

Far to the north, where the sky‑cities drifted like pale islands in the clouds, Lady Aeris Galewing stood on her balcony and watched her people tremble. Sky Elves were not meant to shiver. Their bodies were tuned to the cold, their minds sharp as the winds they commanded. Yet now they lay wrapped in blankets, wings drooping, eyes unfocused.

passages.heading: WrymWretch
passages.text:
A healer approached her, his voice barely above a whisper. “They speak of voices in the wind. They say the stars are calling them by name.”

Aeris had heard the voices too. Soft at first, then insistent. A whisper threading through the clouds: Remember me.

The Priests of the Gale summoned her to the storm chamber. Lightning flickered across the crystalline walls as they spoke of omens, of sickness, of something brushing against the minds of the living. Aeris was chosen to descend from the sky and seek aid from the other realms.

As she prepared her sky‑sail, she looked once more at her people—fevered, trembling, whispering to unseen stars. Something ancient was stirring, and it was reaching for them.

In the deep southern forests, Elder Rhyla Mosswhisper knelt before the Heartstone. The crystal’s glow, once steady as the earth’s pulse, flickered like a dying ember. She placed her palms upon it, and a tremor ran through her bones.

passages.heading: WrymWretch
passages.text:
The vision struck her like a blow: a prison without walls, a name dissolving into silence, a cosmic shape pressing against the veil of existence. She gasped and pulled her hands away. The Heartstone dimmed further, as though exhausted by the effort of remembering.

“Not yet,” she whispered. “You cannot fade. Not now.”

But the crystal knew the truth. Its power was tied to memory, and memory was being erased.

Rhyla rose, leaning heavily on her staff. She would journey to the Deep Core, where the oldest crystals slept. If any wisdom remained, it would be there.

Along the eastern shores, Lunessa Tidecaller waded into water that should have been alive with darting fish and swirling light. Instead, the sea lay still—murky, heavy, suffocating. She dipped her hand beneath the surface, and the water clung to her skin like oil.

Behind her, the elders murmured in fear. The ocean was losing its memory of life.

passages.heading: WrymWretch
passages.text:
Later, lantern‑crystals strapped to her belt, Lunessa descended into the depths with the divers. The water grew darker, colder, heavier. Shapes moved in the gloom—shapes that did not belong to the sea.

At the bottom, half‑buried in silt, she found a monolith carved with symbols her mind refused to hold. Every time she tried to read them, the meaning slid away like a dream upon waking.

She surfaced screaming.

In the Underworld, Kael Duskbane pushed open the stone door of the forbidden chamber. Dust swirled. Candles flared. The prophecy lay open on a pedestal of bone.

When the last memory fades, the Astral Architect shall rise.

Kael’s blood ran cold. He had heard the name once, whispered by a dying sage: Shallock Izladar. A name the world was trying to forget.

He closed the tome and drew his blade. Someone was erasing memories. Someone was killing witnesses.

Kael would hunt them.

passages.heading: WrymWretch
passages.text:
High above the world, in the star‑lit halls of the Luminary Priory, Scholar Seraphyne watched the constellations flicker like dying embers. The heavens were unraveling. She traced the patterns with trembling fingers, and the stars formed a sigil she had hoped never to see again.

The Sigil of Izladar.

She summoned the Priory. Their faces were grim.

“The prison weakens,” she said. “The cosmos trembles. The Remnants move in shadow.”

“And the name?” an elder asked.

passages.heading: Seraphyne hesitated. “Already fading.”
passages.text:
And far beyond all realms, where the land cracked open into a vast abyss of swirling astral winds, WrymWretch stirred.

The bones of ancient wyrms hummed with a resonance not heard in millennia. A ripple of light tore across the chasm, illuminating the cliffs in ghostly fire. From the depths came a voice—distant, echoing, half‑formed.

passages.heading: I… remember… me…
passages.text:
The world shuddered.

The first seal had cracked.

Act I Ends.

ACT II — THE AWAKENING OF THE TWIN SOULS

The night after the forest’s first forgetting, Thalen could not sleep. The Cedarheart Enclave was restless; even the leaves seemed to whisper in uneasy spirals. Sylvan lay coiled beneath the great elder‑tree, its massive form half‑hidden by vines that grew and shifted with its breath. The dragon’s presence steadied the forest, but only barely. The corruption pulsed at the edges of the grove like a bruise.

Thalen sat beside Sylvan’s flank, feeling the warmth of the dragon’s heartbeat through the bark‑like scales. His own pulse matched it, as it always had. He had known since childhood that he was different — that the forest spoke to him in ways it didn’t to others, that vines curled toward his hands, that animals watched him with knowing eyes. But he had never understood why.

passages.heading: I… remember… me…
passages.text:
Now he did.

Sylvan’s voice entered his mind like a breeze through leaves.

You were born when I was born. You breathed when I breathed. You are my other half, Thalen Cedarheart.

passages.heading: He swallowed hard. “And the rot?”
passages.text:
Sylvan’s green eyes dimmed.

It is not rot. It is memory dying. And if memory dies… so do we.

A tremor ran through the forest. The vines around Sylvan tightened protectively.

The others are awakening, Sylvan murmured. The bond calls to them. The world calls to them.

passages.heading: Thalen stood, heart pounding. “Then we must go.”
passages.text:
Sylvan unfurled its wings, and the forest bowed as the twin souls rose into the night.

Aeris Galewing felt the change before she saw it. The winds shifted, spiraling upward in a column of shimmering air. Her lungs tightened, her vision blurred, and for a moment she felt weightless — as if her body remembered how to be something else.

Aetherius descended through the clouds, runes glowing along its parchment‑colored scales. The dragon’s presence calmed the storm inside her chest. She felt the bond lock into place — a sensation like a forgotten melody returning.

“You’re real,” she whispered, though she had always known.

Aetherius lowered its head, touching its snout to her forehead.

We were born together, Aeris. You are the breath I cannot take. I am the thought you cannot speak.

Her knees weakened. “The sickness in the sky‑cities… is it because of me?”

Because of us, Aetherius corrected gently. Our bond was dormant too long. The winds are confused. The stars are remembering things they should not.

passages.heading: Thalen stood, heart pounding. “Then we must go.”
passages.text:
Aeris looked north, where the constellations flickered like dying embers.

“Then we fly.”

Aetherius lifted her onto its back, and together they soared into the night, leaving silver trails across the sky.

Deep beneath the earth, Rhyla Mosswhisper reached the Heartstone Cavern just as the tremors began. Crystals shattered along the walls, their light dimming to ash. The ground split open, revealing a chamber she had never seen — a chamber that pulsed with molten light.

Gaia emerged from the fissure like a mountain waking from sleep.

The dragon’s scales glowed with the colors of stone and soil, and its eyes burned with ancient memory. Rhyla felt her bones resonate with its presence. Her breath synced with its rumbling exhale.

“You came,” she whispered.

Gaia’s voice echoed through her mind like shifting tectonic plates.

We are one, Rhyla. When the earth remembers, I remember. When the earth forgets… we both fall.

passages.heading: Thalen stood, heart pounding. “Then we must go.”
passages.text:
Rhyla touched the dragon’s snout, feeling the warmth of magma beneath the scales.

“The crystals are dying.”

Because the world is losing its story, Gaia replied. And something is stealing the ending.

The cavern shook violently. Dust rained from the ceiling.

We must go south, Gaia said. To the place where the first stones were laid. The others will meet us there.

Rhyla climbed onto Gaia’s back, and together they plunged into the tunnels, leaving the dying crystals behind.

Lunessa Tidecaller stood on the shoreline, staring at the dark water. The sea had always been her comfort, her teacher, her home. But now it felt foreign — as if the tides themselves were grieving.

A ripple broke the surface.

Then another.

Then a massive shape rose from the depths, water cascading off iridescent blue scales. Aquatica emerged with a roar that shook the shoreline, its wings unfurling like the fins of a colossal leviathan.

passages.heading: Thalen stood, heart pounding. “Then we must go.”
passages.text:
Lunessa felt her heart stop.

Her skin shimmered with the same blue glow as the dragon’s scales. Her breath synced with the rhythm of the waves. She felt the bond snap into place — a tidal pull deep in her chest.

“Aquatica,” she whispered.

The dragon’s voice flowed into her mind like a current.

Little tidecaller… you are my other half. And the sea is forgetting us.

Lunessa’s eyes filled with tears. “The monolith I found… it erased itself from my mind.”

Not erased, Aquatica corrected. Devoured.

The sea surged behind them, waves rising unnaturally high.

We must go east, Aquatica said. To the place where the moon first touched the water.

Lunessa climbed onto the dragon’s back, and together they dove beneath the waves.

Kael Duskbane moved through the Underworld tunnels with silent precision, his obsidian skin blending into the shadows. He felt the presence before he saw it — a cold ripple in the air, a whisper of darkness that matched the rhythm of his own heartbeat.

passages.heading: Thalen stood, heart pounding. “Then we must go.”
passages.text:
Umbra stepped from the shadows like a living eclipse.

The dragon’s violet eyes glowed with predatory intelligence. Its scales absorbed the torchlight, swallowing it whole. Kael felt the bond snap into place — a surge of shadow through his veins, a clarity he had never known.

Umbra circled him, its tail brushing the stone.

You have hunted alone too long, Kael, the dragon whispered into his mind. We were born together. We kill together.

Kael’s jaw tightened. “The prophecy speaks of an Astral Architect.”

Shallock Izladar, Umbra hissed. A name the world is trying to forget. A name someone is trying to erase.

passages.heading: Kael nodded. “Then we hunt the Remnants.”
passages.text:
Umbra’s wings unfurled, shadows spilling across the cavern.

And we start at #Wrymreach.

High above the world, in the luminous forests of the High Realm, Seraphyne felt the stars pulse beneath her skin. She staggered, gripping a crystalline tree for support. Her vision blurred, filled with swirling constellations.

A beam of starlight struck the clearing.

Astraia descended in a cascade of shimmering cosmic dust, wings glowing with iridescent light. The dragon’s presence filled the air with warmth and gravity, as if the cosmos itself had taken form.

Seraphyne fell to her knees.

Astraia lowered its head, touching its forehead to hers.

We are one soul split by the moon’s sorrow, the dragon whispered. And the stars are crying out. The prison weakens. The Architect stirs.

passages.heading: Seraphyne’s breath trembled. “Then we must go.”
passages.text:
To #Wrymreach, Astraia said. Where the sun’s anger and the moon’s tear first collided. Where the King of Dragons and Queen of Elves once stood together.

Seraphyne climbed onto Astraia’s back, and the dragon launched into the sky, leaving a trail of starlight behind.

Across the world, six dragons and six elves moved toward the same place.

Toward the abyss where reality thinned.

Toward the birthplace of their kind.

Toward #Wrymreach.

And deep within that chasm, something ancient stirred — a voice half‑formed, a memory refusing to die.

passages.heading: I… remember… me…
passages.text:
The second seal cracked.

The world shuddered.

Act II ends.

#WrymWretch Chapter One — The Shore Between Worlds

The bottles woke him before the light did.

They rolled across the cabin floor in a clattering, off‑key xylophone of glass and regret, chiming with every swell of the sea. The old boat rocked gently, as if trying to soothe him, but the motion only stirred the thunder in his skull. He lay there a moment, eyes half‑open, watching the ceiling beams sway like slow pendulums. The air smelled of salt, rum, and the faint ghost of last night’s pipe smoke.

The walls around him were crowded with the artifacts of a life lived in restless devotion: sketches pinned beside foreign poems, photographs curling at the edges, maps annotated in a hurried hand. Shelves sagged under the weight of books from ports he barely remembered leaving. Cabinets rattled with jars of spices and teas collected like talismans from far‑off markets. Every inch of the cabin carried the evidence of a man who had never learned to travel lightly.

passages.heading: I… remember… me…
passages.text:
He exhaled, long and ragged, and only then noticed the bottle still in his hand. A few amber drops clung to the bottom like stubborn memories. He set it aside and pushed himself upright, the familiar ache of a seasoned hangover settling behind his eyes. This was not the clumsy rise of a novice drunk; this was the practiced, almost graceful ascent of a man who had greeted many dawns in this exact condition.

The light outside was shifting. Thin threads of orange stretched across the porthole, weaving themselves into the gold of early morning. He blinked at it, squinting as though the sun were an adversary he had not prepared to face.

With a soft groan, he stood and made his way through the cluttered cabin, stepping over scattered notes and half‑finished sketches. The stairs creaked beneath his weight as he climbed to the deck.

The world greeted him with a hush.

passages.heading: I… remember… me…
passages.text:
The sea was calm, a pane of molten gold reflecting the newborn sky. The shoreline lay not far off—a quiet crescent of pale sand, untouched and waiting. He stared at it with bleary, unfocused eyes, as though trying to remember why it mattered. Something in him stirred. A pull. A promise he couldn’t name.

Before he could think better of it, he swung himself over the rail and dropped into the dinghy tied alongside. The small boat rocked, then steadied. He took up the oars with the muscle memory of a man who had crossed many uncertain waters, and began to row.

The journey was short, but each stroke felt like a negotiation with the remnants of last night’s rum. The dinghy slid onto the sand with a soft, wet squelch. He stepped out, boots sinking slightly into the cool grit.

He walked toward the place where the tide kissed the shore—a narrow, shimmering boundary between sea and land. The air there felt different, charged with something he couldn’t name. He paused, letting the waves lap at his ankles, letting the morning settle around him.

passages.heading: I… remember… me…
passages.text:
For a moment, he simply stood in that liminal space, neither fully arrived nor fully departed.

A man between worlds.

A man on the edge of remembering something important.

And the day, still young and golden, waited to see what he would do next.

passages.heading: Chapter Two — The Princess on the Shore
passages.text:
His feet sank into the sand with a wet, sucking sound, each step a slow negotiation with the earth. My toes—his toes—had long since grown rough from the constant embrace of salt and grit, the sea forever sculpting them into something less human and more… tidal. He trudged forward with the heavy, deliberate gait of a man who had only recently remembered he possessed legs at all. The tide had retreated moments before, leaving the beach slick and gleaming, as though he were walking across the exposed ribs of the ocean itself.

Then came the voice.

“Alexi!”

Smooth. Sweet. Too clean for this wild place. It drifted over the tropical wind like a ribbon of perfume—synthetic pineapple and coconut, the unmistakable scent of someone who had never once applied her own sunscreen. Even the breeze carried the memory of hands that had rubbed lotion into royal shoulders.

He turned toward it, blinking through the haze of rum and morning light. And then—because instinct is faster than thought—he rushed toward the sound.

passages.heading: Chapter Two — The Princess on the Shore
passages.text:
Well, “rushed” is generous. He lurched. He zigzagged. He performed what future scholars might generously describe as a bold and experimental interpretation of running. But he moved with purpose, and that counts for something.

He stopped a little too late.

Which is to say: he didn’t stop at all.

He collided with her—a small, startled figure in a pale dress—and the two of them went down in a tangle of limbs, sand, and royal disbelief. Her dress, once pristine, now bore the full signature of the beach. And some say his hands, in the chaos of the fall, traveled further than any man’s had before—for she was a princess, after all, and princesses are not accustomed to being tackled by hungover sailors at dawn.

He scrambled backward, found his balance, lost it again, and collapsed into something that might have been a bow, or a grovel, or a man attempting to fold himself into a shape the gods would find amusing.

passages.heading: Chapter Two — The Princess on the Shore
passages.text:
“Your Highness,” he managed, though it came out sounding more like “Yer Hine‑ness.”

She sat up, brushing sand from her sleeves with the resigned grace of someone who had long ago accepted that her life would never be normal. Her eyes—sharp, ocean‑colored, and far too awake for this hour—fixed on him.

“Alexi,” she said, “I bring a warning.”

Of course she did. Warnings always arrive when a man is least prepared to receive them. Even the waves seemed to pause, listening.

“My father’s debts have grown too great,” she continued. “He has sold his halls to the Great British Tea Company. And now the Lord of Tea has set his eyes on the ocean.”

passages.heading: Alexi blinked. “Tea has a lord.”
passages.text:
“Everything has a lord,” she said. “But this one… he is hungry. He wants every ship, every vessel, every soul that sails. He wants to turn the ocean into his fleet. He will drain the empire, and then the people, until all that remains is a wasteland of scraps and ash.”

The wind shifted. The scent of pineapple faded. Something colder took its place.

Alexi felt the weight settle on him—not the weight of her words, but the weight of what they meant. The world tilting. The tide pulling back. The kind of moment a man remembers long after he has forgotten his own name.

He imagined a life without the sea.

A life where no one knew the warm blush of sunrise over open water.  
Where no one tasted the salt on the rim of a bottle weathered by storms.  
Where no one sang drunken hymns to the tide, praising her like a lover who always returned.  
Where the ocean was not a wild, living thing—but a factory, a fleet, a machine.

passages.heading: Alexi blinked. “Tea has a lord.”
passages.text:
He felt it like a punch to the ribs.

And somewhere deep inside him—somewhere older than memory, older than the man he had become—something stirred. Something that knew the sea was not meant to be owned.

The princess watched him, waiting.

The waves whispered their own warning.

And I—who am him and not him, who walk beside him and inside him—felt the first tremor of the story that would swallow us whole.

works.title: Through the Eyes of Wolf and Lamb
works.blurb: A complicit narrator's satirical, self-indicting quartet about how institutions launder violence into language.

passages.heading: Through the Eyes of Wolf and Lamb
passages.text:
Through the Eyes of Wolf and Lamb

Content warning: this book satirizes institutions, language, and the stories we tell about violence. It refers to harm and culpability but does not describe methods or revel in injury. If you need to step away at any point, do so.

I write this as a set of promises and as an experiment. A reader deserves to know the rules before they enter a house whose rooms are lit by irony and whose windows sometimes show things you would rather not see. I also want to test whether a voice can hold both a joke and a wound, whether satire can indict without erasing, whether a ledger can be a kind of mercy.

passages.heading: Through the Eyes of Wolf and Lamb
passages.text:
I will not use real names, ongoing cases, or private details of people who have suffered. I will not provide instruction, technique, or anything that could be taken as a how‑to. I will not make victims into props for cleverness; they will have interior lives, small habits, and the dignity of being more than plot points. I will aim my satire at systems—press releases, checklists, risk assessments, the language of mitigation—and at the human vanity that dresses itself in procedure.

These are not legal shields. They are not moral absolutions. They are, at best, the scaffolding of an ethical experiment: can a writer hold a mirror up to the machinery that makes harm legible without becoming part of that machinery?

Four is a shape that feels like a sentence: setup, escalation, chorus, reckoning. One book to show the private ledger; one to show the public forms; one to show the witnesses and the rumor economy; one to show the aftermath and the market for remorse. Four books let me move from intimacy to spectacle and back again without stretching the conceit into a carnival.

passages.heading: Through the Eyes of Wolf and Lamb
passages.text:
Expect an unreliable intimacy. Expect lists and receipts, memos and mock press releases. Expect a voice that can be charming and then, in the next breath, cold. Expect irony that is not a shield but a scalpel: it cuts to reveal the rot beneath the varnish. Expect omissions. Sometimes what I do not say will be the loudest thing in the room.

If you have read this far trusting me, then I have done my job as a rhetorician. If you have read this far suspicious of me, then I have done my job as a provocateur. Both are useful states for what follows.

There is a paragraph I could have placed elsewhere, but I put it here because the foreword is the place where a narrator can be most theatrical about ethics. I will be theatrical now.

I have been present at scenes that will appear in these pages. I have read the forms that will appear as epigraphs. I have signed the letters that will be quoted. I have, in small and large ways, been part of the machinery that turns private harm into public language. I do not mean this as a boast. I do not mean it as a confession in the legal sense. I mean it as a fact of proximity. Proximity is not innocence. Proximity is not guilt. Proximity is a kind of responsibility that sits in the throat like a stone.

passages.heading: Through the Eyes of Wolf and Lamb
passages.text:
I remember a blue mug. I remember washing it once because the handle fit my thumb the way a small kindness fits a day; I remember the sound the spoon made against the ceramic. That sound is why I could not pretend distance. That sound is why the admission in this foreword is not an abstract gesture but a personal ledger entry.

You will find, in the second book, a killer who keeps lists. You will find, in the third, a chorus of witnesses who misremember and misreport. You will find, in the fourth, the market for apologies and the ledger of what can and cannot be repaired. Read them now with the knowledge that the person who wrote the disclaimers is not a neutral observer. Read them knowing that the voice that promises dignity has, at times, been the voice that helped translate dignity into a line item.

This is not a plea for forgiveness. It is not a demand for absolution. It is a refusal to hide behind the convenient fiction that satire is always a higher ground. I have been on the ground. I have seen how the forms we invent to manage risk can become the very instruments that obscure harm. I have seen how a press release can be a kind of erasure. I have seen how a checklist can be a way of not looking.

passages.heading: Through the Eyes of Wolf and Lamb
passages.text:
If you are looking for a narrator who will be pure, you will not find one here. If you are looking for a narrator who will be honest about the ways language can wound and the ways language can be used to avoid responsibility, then you will find that here, in awkward measures.

There will be moments in these books when the humor is sharp and the satire lands. There will be moments when the humor is a thin veneer over something that is not funny at all. Those moments are intentional. They are the point. Satire that only amuses is a party trick. Satire that unsettles asks a question of the reader: what do you do with the knowledge that the teller is not innocent?

I will end this foreword not with a defense but with a ledger entry—small, precise, and unadorned—because the books that follow are full of lists and because lists are how we try to make sense of what we cannot fully understand.

passages.heading: Through the Eyes of Wolf and Lamb
passages.text:
Ledger entry: I was there. I wrote the forms. I signed the letters. I watched the language do its work. I will not tell you how to harm. I will tell you how we made harm legible, how we packaged it, how we sold it back to ourselves as something manageable.

Read the quartet as a confession and as a critique. Read it as a satire that turns inward. Read it as an experiment in whether a voice that has been complicit can still be useful in naming the systems that made complicity possible.

I wrote the rules so you would trust me. I broke them so you would notice.

•

I begin with a list because lists are how I make the world legible. They are tidy, finite, and they let me pretend that consequence is a checkbox. Today’s list is ordinary: milk, batteries, call the landlord, pick up the suit. I write the items in a small notebook with a pen that leaves a faint blue smear when I press too hard. The smear is a kind of signature; it tells me I was here.

passages.heading: Through the Eyes of Wolf and Lamb
passages.text:
I narrate myself as someone who notices details. I notice the way the coffee shop’s loyalty app calls a free pastry a “customer appreciation gesture.” I notice the way the local paper rewrites grief into a headline that fits a template. I notice the way people say the word “incident” as if it were a neutral weather event.

There is a pleasure in the ritual of checking things off. The pleasure is not the same as joy. It is a small, private economy of control.

A receipt folded into a pocket: wholegrain bread; two bananas; note: call Mom on Thursday. The handwriting on the note is slanted, quick, the kind of slant that belongs to someone who writes lists to outrun forgetting.

I rehearse explanations in the shower. Explanations are like scripts; they keep the voice steady when the world wants to shout. I practice the tone that will sound reasonable in a press conference: contrite, measured, forward-looking. I practice the sentence that will make people nod and then forget.

passages.heading: Through the Eyes of Wolf and Lamb
passages.text:
My mind arranges motives into tidy categories: stress, miscommunication, a lapse. Motives are useful because they make moral complexity look like a spreadsheet. I like spreadsheets. Spreadsheets have columns and totals and a final cell that sums everything up.

A voicemail saved on a cracked phone: “Hey, it’s me. Don’t forget the plant. Water it on Friday. Also—if you get a minute—call me back. I found a place that does pottery classes.” The voice at the end laughs, small and private.

I tell myself that language is a tool and that tools can be repurposed. I take the language of care and bend it into policy. I draft a memo about boundaries that reads like a love letter to procedure. I write: We must balance empathy with operational integrity. It is a sentence that sounds like both a promise and a disclaimer.

There is a small, comic distance between the person who writes memos and the person who lives inside them. The memo author believes in systems. The person who lives inside them believes in outcomes. I am both.

passages.heading: Through the Eyes of Wolf and Lamb
passages.text:
A half-finished letter found in a drawer: “…and if you ever come by, bring the blue mug. I keep thinking of the way the light hits the sink in the morning. I miss the way you hum when you’re making coffee. If this is the last letter I write, know that I kept your postcards in a shoebox under the bed.” The sentence stops as if interrupted by something ordinary and then not.

Humor is a defense mechanism and a rhetorical strategy. I use it to soften edges, to make the reader lean in. I tell jokes about forms and about the absurdity of checkboxes labeled Mitigated. The jokes land because they are true: mitigation is often a verb we use to make ourselves feel less culpable.

I begin to notice the gaps. The victim’s handwriting on the receipt is a different rhythm than the memos I write. The voicemail’s laugh is a sound I cannot replicate. The half-finished letter contains a tenderness that resists translation into policy.

passages.heading: Through the Eyes of Wolf and Lamb
passages.text:
A photograph tucked into a book: two people at a fair, one with a paper crown askew, both squinting into the sun. On the back: June 12. Best day for cotton candy. The ink has faded at the edges.

The checklist grows teeth. Items that once fit neatly into boxes now resist categorization. Apologize is not a checkbox. Make amends is not a line item. I try to write them as such anyway. I draft a form: Restorative Action Request. It has fields for sincerity, for timeline, for measurable outcomes. The form feels ridiculous and necessary at once.

I begin to feel the weight of proximity as a physical thing, like a stone in the throat. It is not guilt in the melodramatic sense. It is the slow recognition that language can be used to tidy away a person.

A grocery list with a doodle in the margin: eggs, coffee, soap and a small sketch of a cat with one ear bent. The doodle is the kind of thing you make when you are thinking of someone else and the world is otherwise ordinary.

passages.heading: Through the Eyes of Wolf and Lamb
passages.text:
I tell myself the truth in small increments. The truth is not a single, dramatic confession; it is a series of adjustments to tone, to omission, to what I choose to emphasize. I begin to see my own voice in the memos I wrote. I see the same rhetorical moves: the passive construction, the appeal to process, the invocation of “lessons learned.”

There is a moment—quiet, almost bureaucratic—when I realize that the forms I drafted did not merely describe a world; they helped make it. The checklist did not only record risk; it taught people how to think about risk. The language of mitigation became a way to avoid looking.

A voicemail, older: “Don’t forget to laugh today. Even if it’s small. Even if it’s at something dumb on TV. Promise me you’ll laugh.” The promise is a small, human insistence.

Midweek, I write a memo titled “Boundaries and Care.” It is careful, the kind of document that will later be praised for its balance. Two days later, a press release uses the same sentence: “We are committed to learning and to doing better.” I see the line on the news and recognize my own phrasing repurposed as corporate absolution. The recognition is a small, cold thing.

passages.heading: Through the Eyes of Wolf and Lamb
passages.text:
There is a chapter where the checklist unravels. The list becomes a single paragraph of breathless fragments: milk, batteries, the way the light used to fall, the way I pretended not to hear, the pen that smudges blue, the sound of a spoon, the sentence I keep erasing and then writing again until the paper looks like a palimpsest of excuses. The paragraph is a fissure. It is the moment the tidy voice cracks.

I begin to notice the manuscript itself. I keep drafts in a shared folder. One night I open a file labeled FOREWORD_FINAL.docx and find my sentences rearranged. The top of the page reads “COMMUNICATIONS HOLD: Key Messages.” A paragraph I wrote about light in the kitchen has been replaced by a checklist titled “Apology Talking Points.” My cursor blinks in the margin where a new sentence—cold, procedural—has been pasted. The file properties show a later timestamp and a device name I do not recognize: COMM-LAPTOP. I print the page and the paper smells faintly of coffee and toner. In the margin, in a hand that is not mine, someone has written: We will learn and grow.

passages.heading: Through the Eyes of Wolf and Lamb
passages.text:
There are marginal notes in the printed drafts. My neat, looping hand appears beside a sentence: (emphasize dignity; avoid sensationalism) — 3/12 09:14. Beneath it, in blocky capitals, a later note: We will learn and grow. — added 3/13 02:07, device: COMM-LAPTOP. The handwriting is different. The tone is different. The insertion reads like an occupation.

I take the printed draft to the office copier because I want to see the physical evidence. The copier jams. When I open the tray, a sheet falls out with a paragraph glued in, the glue still tacky. Someone has physically pasted a new paragraph into my manuscript. The glue leaves a faint sheen on the paper. The act is small and intimate and violent in the way a theft can be.

At a PR meeting I watch language being chosen to erase a person. A junior comms person says, “We should say their name. We can’t keep calling it ‘the incident.’” The counsel taps a pen. “Names complicate liability,” she says. “We need a line that reassures stakeholders.” The junior opens their mouth and closes it. The final statement reads: We are deeply saddened by recent events. The choice is not accidental. Erasure is a policy decision.

passages.heading: Through the Eyes of Wolf and Lamb
passages.text:
The town hums with ordinary life until a series of small absences—missed shifts, an unanswered voicemail, a canceled pottery class—becomes a public story. The witnesses assemble themselves like a chorus: the barista who remembers a laugh, the cop who files the wrong box, the neighbor who swears they saw nothing, the influencer who turns grief into content. Each vignette is a shard of truth and a mirror of omission.

The barista rewrites a customer’s order in a notebook; later the same notebook contains a line that reads like a checklist rather than a memory. The cop files a report under PROPERTY instead of PERSON because the form looked similar and the day was long; the misfiling becomes a motif for institutional mis-seeing. The influencer posts a clip that reframes grief as spectacle; comments and metrics drown out testimony.

The misfiled box is a small, tactile thing. The clerk’s fingers hesitate on the tape. The label reads PROPERTY in a hand that had once been neat; someone has scrawled PERSON in a different ink. She breathes dust into the room and feels the weight of the folder like a small animal. “I thought it was paperwork,” she says later, voice small. “I didn’t think it would be a person.” When the box is opened, the smell of old paper and dust rises. Inside are a receipt, a photograph, a voicemail transcription. The items are not new. They are only newly visible.

passages.heading: Through the Eyes of Wolf and Lamb
passages.text:
At the community meeting the vignettes converge. Official reports, viral clips, and private testimonies are read aloud. The meeting becomes a theater of authorship: who gets to narrate the event, and whose voice will be believed? One witness reads an unedited fragment from my original manuscript—an honest, unadorned sentence that refuses the checklist’s grammar—and the room goes quiet. For a moment the town hears the difference between being described and being named.

The manuscript fragments in the margins begin to show a struggle. My neat notes—(emphasize dignity; avoid sensationalism)—are followed by blocky insertions that read like directives. I find deleted lines in the file history: a sentence naming the person removed, a paragraph about light in the kitchen replaced by a paragraph about lessons learned. I try to restore the original text. My edits reappear overwritten. The timestamps tell a story: my draft at 09:14; an insertion at 02:07 from a device labeled COMM-LAPTOP. The takeover is not metaphoric. It is logged.

passages.heading: Through the Eyes of Wolf and Lamb
passages.text:
The hearing is advertised as accountability. It is scheduled in a municipal auditorium with a livestream link and a press table. The clerk who misfiled the box testifies. She speaks in a voice that is small and honest. She says she misread a label. She says she filed a folder under property because the form looked like property. She says she did not think the difference mattered.

A lawyer objects. A headline runs: Procedural Error Hampers Case. The livestream chat fills with shorthand outrage and performative grief. The hearing admits evidence in technical terms. A key witness statement is excluded because it arrived one day late. The misfiled box is found in a storage room behind a stack of old risk assessments. The items inside are not new. They are only newly visible. The hearing produces a ruling that is procedural rather than moral. There is no criminal conviction. There is a civil settlement with nondisclosure clauses. There is a press release template that the killer’s team circulates to partners. The town watches a legal grammar protect a person more than it serves the harmed.

passages.heading: Through the Eyes of Wolf and Lamb
passages.text:
Interleaved with the hearing are the victim’s reconstructed entries: small domestic facts that refuse to be flattened. I kept lists because lists were how I remembered to be alive. Bread. Water. Call the neighbor about the mail. The lists are small things. They are not heroic. They are the shape of a life. I liked the blue mug because it fit my hand. I liked the way the cat slept on the radiator in winter. If you want to know me, start there.

When they asked me to describe the day, I told them about the light in the kitchen. They wanted a timeline. I gave them a timeline and then I gave them the light. The timeline fit into a box on a form. The light did not.

I do not want my life to be a lesson. I want it to be a person. If you must tell a story, tell the small ones: the postcard kept in a shoebox, the laugh that came before the sentence. Those are the things that do not translate into press releases.

passages.heading: Through the Eyes of Wolf and Lamb
passages.text:
Restitution arrives in forms that look like choices. A corporate donation is announced with a logo and a pledge to fund mental health initiatives. A grassroots fund is started by neighbors to pay for counseling and to maintain a small memorial. A restorative circle convenes in a church basement with no cameras and no press releases. People speak. People listen. The circle produces no legal remedy but it produces names and promises and a plan to check in.

The killer signs a book deal. The advance is publicized as a way to fund the settlement. The killer goes on a podcast tour. The interviews are edited to emphasize learning. The market for remorse is brisk. Publishers call it a necessary conversation. Critics call it commodified contrition. The killer’s life continues with new income streams and curated vulnerability.

The community’s appetite for closure is uneven. Some accept the settlement and the garden fund. Some refuse the hush clauses and demand public naming. Some want the killer to be shunned. Some want to move on. The town fractures along these lines. The fracture is not dramatic. It is a slow, social erosion: friendships that once were easy become careful; neighborhood barbecues have a seat left empty.

passages.heading: Through the Eyes of Wolf and Lamb
passages.text:
I decide to reclaim the pen. I publish an annotated edition of the killer’s memoir excerpts alongside the unedited fragments of the foreword. The side-by-side exposes rhetorical sleights: passive voice, euphemism, the conversion of personhood into lesson. The annotations are not vindictive. They are forensic. They show how language was used to sanitize and to sell.

I testify at a public forum, not as an expert but as someone who watched their own voice be colonized. I read aloud the sentence that began the foreword before the invasion: I will not make victims into props. The room listens. The reading is small and precise. It is a reclaiming.

A garden is planted on a strip of municipal land that had been a vacant lot. The garden is funded by small donations, by the grassroots fund, and by neighbors who bring shovels and seedlings. There is no ribbon-cutting with the killer on stage. There is a bench with a plaque that names the person who is gone and lists three small facts: the blue mug, the cat with the bent ear, the postcard shoebox.

passages.heading: Through the Eyes of Wolf and Lamb
passages.text:
The killer walks by on the other side of the street, a figure in a crowd, not confronted, not forgiven. The killer’s apology has been rehearsed; the garden’s work is not. The victim’s sister kneels in the soil and presses a seed into the earth. She does not speak into a microphone. She does not sign a release. She plants.

Before the planting, a diary fragment is read aloud: “I like the blue mug because it fits my thumb. If I forget everything else, remember the mug.” The sentence is small and stubborn. It refuses the ledger’s grammar.

I sit on the bench with a notebook and a pen that leaves a faint blue smear when pressed too hard. The smear is a kind of signature. I write one sentence, unadorned and final.

We planted what we could; the rest we learned to name.

works.title: The Cycle of Us
works.blurb: One soul-line lived across nine reincarnations, from a drowned boy to a healed, peaceful final self.

passages.heading: The Cycle of Us
passages.text:
The Cycle of Us

the story starts with 9 people standing in a room sharing the same face but all wearing it differently. The background a blurred haze begins to take shape like sand shifting with the sea the void empty white space giving shape to nine paths that loom distantly on the horizon. Their lives call them earnestly, beckoning with voices so sweet they caress the very vail of nostalgic moments gently pull each of them away as they walk towards their respective lives falling back in as if the end had never came.

The first life  
He lived his life to the fullest. Running, dancing, filling the air with laughter far before he’d grown old enough to ponder the worries of tomorrow. When one day while him and his brother where at play by the sea his brother slip, fell, and got washed out further than the his eyes could see but he bravely jumped summoning strength like no other to save him. He gets to his brother fighting the current and helps him get close to shore but he can’t save himself as his brother drifts with another current back to the shore where he later wakes up he is washed further and further out. Where for a time he tries to fight but it is no use and as he slips from the surface he sees a school of fish surrounding him and as his body goes stiff and lifeless, his eyes clenching the finale lingers of light as his last breathe fails and his lungs fill with water. He could’ve sworn that right before he died it was peaceful the school of fish’s bright scales reflected the light make him feel like an angelic choir surrounded him in his ascent from this earth.

passages.heading: The Cycle of Us
passages.text:
In the rest of the 8 he learned never to fear the water for no other moment filled him with such peace as the first time his soul died, he felt that no other end would bring such stillness of the mind. His brother lived on and he carried his late brothers spirit with him where he was rebirthed in his grandson.

(The Second Life)  
The boy had watched his father sit on the bench watching his children play his whole childhood. His grandfather had made that bench in memorial of his late brother who died saving his life. My grandfather had moved away with his parents shortly after, they moved to the big city with no large body of water around. I think it scared my grandfather but he moved back to the beach and learned to swim again. He taught my dad to be a strong swimmer and now me. Some days I sit on this bench to feel him close to me. My grandfather said I reminded him of his brother and it made me want to be like him (my late great uncle, former reincarnation).  After the passing of my grandfather I became very close to my father. I lived in his shadow: observing him, nurturing him, watching as he aged beyond reckoning and his mind faded, I watched the grey slowly bleach his hair, leach into the color of his eyes, and in the end paint the complexion of his face as we closed his casket on that faithful we all come to grow quite close to even if we are scared of death. For me this moment felt more sacred than a birthday because this was the final page not the beginning. I wish I could’ve said this was the end of my story in his shadow but it was not. It was only after his death my mother told me about him before he was kind and gentle. When they first met he had a crippling relationship with his father (my grandfather, and past life brother). My grandfather had struggled with control after the death of his brother and that control crushed the young spirit of my father. When my mother met him he was unpredictable snapping from anger to deep isolation. He drank heavily, gambled his life with bad people he owed debts to, and in the end almost lost my mother before I was born because he had let the relationship with his father grow so stale. They never talked even though they only had each other, grandma left grandpa after he drove off their son and this put grandpa into bad health, my father couldn’t fight his feelings anymore after his father fell ill. He checked himself into AA, he slept by his fathers beside for months as his father fought to live, he found a religion (forgiveness, love, and compassion towards those close to him) that would grow the foundation for our family tree (the linage of this souls 9 reincarnations). I saw my father differently now he wasn’t perfect and the idolization of him had made our time together feel stifled and one sided but now I saw him as more: he wasn’t just my father he shared my path and my flaws, he was me. I started to realize the pattern that was forming around me. I bought my parents house and moved my mother into the upstairs after my father’s passing. She took up knitting, storytelling, and so much more. She bloomed like it was spring everyday of her life but in these later moments after the passing of my father I realized all to later how beautiful of a soul she was. Somewhere in my mind I lamented because of how little I knew about her in my idolization of my father. I spent so many moments breathing in the same air as my father just trying to catch a glimpse of where he found his strength but now I see she was the one who gave life to every breathe he took. I thought back to my life: I built a house hold I had fallen in love with my wife and I had 2 beautiful daughters with one on way, they’re first girls to be born in our line. I knew my fore fathers would be proud just as I was the first time I saw their faces. The innocence of baby girl will make even the strongest men weak with love and protection, there is no sweeter or more innocent sound than their first cries each and every cry touched my heart with a even greater feeling of love till I thought it would stop beating. I looked at my mother differently after I had girls now. She was still young when my father died and so the love my grandfather gave me carried on into my children in a feminine form like that of an all loving mother. I was happy to see such beautiful family roots connecting us all even from the grave. I wish I had taken it in a little more but just as always we learn the truth only when a lie has taken shape.

passages.heading: The third Life
passages.text: I hadn’t been born yet when my father passed. It was a day like any other day my mom told me when I was old enough to handle it, he had taken both of my older sisters to go to a concert, they didn’t make it back a drunk driver hit them head on as they were leaving. My dad and my oldest sister Anna had died first because they were up front but Emily my other sister had made it out ok, or so we thought. The real troubles began in the hospital, Emily didn’t do well after the accident, she had a lot of internal damage but most of all she had been damaged mentally. She would stare out the windows for hours with moving an inch,she hadn’t talked to anyone after she found out that the others had died. I hadn’t come see her much, the doctors managed to keep her sustained but she would most likely never recover. As I got older I could remember reheating leftovers when grandma wasn’t there to make food for me, I was about 8 now and mom hadn’t slept at the house for more than a weekend in that time. She was always at the hospital trying to console my sister and motivate her, I didn’t resent her for this but i didn’t exactly have anyone other than grandma to talk to and she was gone to the hospital only a little less than mom did. When. Grandma was home she would tell me stories of how my great great uncle had saved my great grandpa from drowning, why we live by the sea to remember him and keep him close, and how my father had built our beautiful home with his hard work and how he had saved up enough for us to be safe even when he didn’t plan to be gone. I loved all the stories she would tell me of my family it made me feel close to them but my favorite stories were of my mother, she had told me about how she had taken on 2 day jobs to pay for the medical bills, and put food on the table, she would tell me of the many beautiful dates that her son had taken my mom on, I feel that I learned from both the love my mother had for me and my sister and how my mother loved my father. I thought that I wouldn’t be happy unless I had a love like they did, in my mind it was a love that was parallel to a prince saving a princess. My mother decided one day that I was old enough to come to the hospital and see my sister, I have to admit I was scared to see her after all our time apart and I was still young. When we got to the hospital and we entered the hall towards my sisters room I felt a sense of dread hit my stomach as I could tell something was wrong.  Monitors and alarms blasted over the silence, doctors ran past us hurriedly trying to get to the patient in need of help, I heard my mom gasp and the bottom of my stomach nearly fall out of my body as only a few feet in front of us they swung the door of my sisters room open. What I saw in that quick moment, before me and my mom were swiftly leave the area, scarred me for life. My sister lay in her bed note on the side table and wrists gushing. The following year flew by and it was like I hit a reset. My mom and I had finally adjusted after months of therapy and she worked less and less planning for her early retirement so she could make up the lost time together. I had a weirded epiphany one day after graduating from psychiatric school; my first client walked through the door and it was none other than my mother. She said in a flush of emotion that she had booked my first session anonymously so that I wouldn’t be prepared and we could have this session more naturally. I told her I understood and smiled at her telling her I was proud of her doing this for us. We talked for hours well beyond normal session time, I had to cancel on 3 other clients but this was worth every bit of lost money. I felt so close to her, I understood after this moment that hers and father’s love was far from perfect. She told me he was a great man, he loved with all his heart, gave even to the undeserving, and forgave anyone who ever crossed him but he was distant. She said that she was worried that just like our (mother and daughter)  relationship my father and his father had grown so close there was no room for them to find themselves, he had regretted spending all his life in his fathers shadow and never finding his own path. I don’t want you to do the same, I grasped her hand and said “mom with this life, I’d like to spend it with you. No one else will do, for no one loved us like you.” When I said us I knew I ment my sister and so did my mom, we cried, we spoke words with no movement of mouths other than the cries that welled up from tears, we spoke more vulnerably than we ever had yet not one word was spoken. Something in my soul seemed to be full filled in this life and moment and I knew that in another life I would follow a much different path one carved out something raw and rugged but for this one I would love ever soft warm hug and sob that I could get from the woman who gave me life and filled my already broken heart with more love than I could hold.

passages.heading: The third Life
passages.text:
The Fourth Life — The Brother’s First Stage (Running From Oneself)

The soul that lived Lives 1–3 dissolves, and a new one begins — but the story never announces it.

He was born with a restlessness that didn’t belong to him, a kind of inherited ache that pulsed beneath his ribs like a memory he never lived. His mother said he kicked in the womb like he was trying to outrun something, and when he grew older, he did exactly that.

He ran from town to town, job to job, face to face, never staying long enough to let anyone see the soft, frightened boy beneath the bravado. He didn’t know why he felt like he was being chased by a shadow shaped like grief, or why the ocean made him uneasy even though he’d never lived near one.

He wasn’t dying at the end of this stage — he was shedding.  
The boy who ran could no longer carry the weight of the man he needed to become.

passages.heading: The third Life
passages.text:
The Fifth Life — The Brother’s Second Stage (The 9–5 Life)

Same soul, new phase — but the reader only senses the shift.

He settled into routine as if it were a punishment.  
A desk.  
A clock.  
A life measured in keystrokes and coffee breaks.

He lived quietly, mechanically, as though the world had pressed him into a mold he didn’t choose. But sometimes, when he walked home at dusk, he felt a strange tug — a longing for someone he’d never met, a sense that he was supposed to be part of something larger, something older.

He didn’t know it, but he was feeling the echo of the soul who came before him — the one whose life ended just as his began.

This stage ended not with death, but with a soft cracking inside him, the shell of monotony breaking open.

---

The Sixth Life — The Brother’s Final Stage (Loving Someone Who Didn’t Love Back)

passages.heading: The third Life
passages.text:
The brother’s last transformation before the soul-line passes on.

He loved someone who could not love him back, and in that unreturned devotion he confronted every wound he had inherited — the fear of abandonment, the ache of longing, the quiet belief that he was always one step behind the life he was meant to live.

He poured himself into someone who remained distant, and in that heartbreak he felt something ancient stir — a grief that wasn’t his, a tenderness that didn’t belong to this lifetime.

When this stage ended, he didn’t die.  
He simply reached the limit of who he could be.  
And the soul that had carried him through three transformations dissolved into something new — something softer, something waiting to be born.

---

The Seventh Life — The Sister’s First Stage (Chasing Dreams)

The brother’s soul-line ends, and the sister’s begins — but the story never says this outright.

passages.heading: The third Life
passages.text:
She was born with fire in her chest, a spark that felt older than her bones. She dreamed in colors too bright for the world she lived in, chasing visions that felt like memories from a life she never lived.

She traveled far, not to escape but to seek — though she didn’t know what. Sometimes she felt as though she were running toward someone she had once loved deeply, someone she had never met in this life but missed all the same.

She didn’t know it, but she was carrying the brother’s unfinished longing, transformed into ambition.

This stage ended when she realized that dreams were not destinations but doorways.

---

The Eighth Life — The Sister’s Second Stage (A Life Spent Alone)

The sister’s middle transformation — quieter, deeper.

She withdrew from the world, choosing solitude not out of fear but instinct. She lived near the sea, drawn to it without understanding why, as if the waves whispered stories she had forgotten.

passages.heading: The third Life
passages.text:
She spent her days in silence, tending to a garden that grew wild and unruly. She felt a presence sometimes — a warmth beside her, a shadow that felt protective rather than frightening.

She didn’t know it, but she was feeling the echo of the brother — not as a ghost, but as a memory carried in the bloodline, a tenderness passed down like a family heirloom.

This stage ended when she realized solitude was not loneliness — it was preparation.

---

The Ninth Life — The Sister’s Final Stage (Healing and Peace)

The final transformation — the soul-line completes itself.

She became gentle, luminous, whole.  
She forgave easily.  
She loved slowly.  
She moved through the world with the calm certainty of someone who had carried many versions of herself and finally set them down.

She often sat by the sea on a weathered bench, feeling a presence settle beside her — familiar, steady, protective. She didn’t know why she whispered, “It’s alright now,” but she did. And the wind seemed to answer.

passages.heading: The third Life
passages.text:
She wasn’t speaking to a ghost.  
She was speaking to the lineage — the brother, the soul before him, the entire chain of selves that had led to her.

works.title: The Endless Temple - Elaris Sel Marden
works.blurb: An elf scholar eternally guarding a library of living-universe books reads himself into a desert exile's quest.

passages.heading: The Endless Temple - Elaris Sel Marden
passages.text:
Introduction

…I stood upon the edge of the abyss. The cold bit at my skin as the dark mist swelled around me and overhead. I stared into the darkness, straining my eyes to glimpse something… anything. I stayed motionless for some time, praying that I might see some sign of hope, but no. For in the great darkness, no light can be found…

Books lined the shelves. They covered the floors and tables. Some could even be found in the pantries alongside outlandish fares like goblin's eyes or Ogers’ tongue, all kept bobbing and floating neatly in sealed jars for later consumption. The sun peered in through an open window, and off in the distance, a peculiar cuckoo clock cooed. As the sunbeams stretched across the floor like growing vines of light, they began to touch upon the face of one bizarre creature. Eyes fast shut, holding back golden orbs ornately chiseled by deep brown irises and large, seamlessly bottomless pupils. His pale green skin glistened like sea froth at the first peak of the morning, contrasted by the dark shadows of his room. His limbs, elegant and elongated, lay sprawled about the bed as he wiped his eyes. As he rose, his frame towered above the furnishings in his room; though thin, he stood at almost 8 feet in stature. However, he may not be easily defined by his features or flowing dark locks. His ears quite quickly gave him away as they rose to a point at the top. He was an elf and, by the looks of it, a scholar, for he was draped in monk’s attire. Quickly, he readied himself and left the room, striding into the halls of the endless temple. This was no ordinary temple, nor was it meant for some form of worship to a higher power or home to great beings. This temple was created to protect and oversee the countless worlds safely stowed within, for every book was alive, and inside of it, an entire universe. Each microcosm had its own stories, myths, legends, and even microcosms of its own. This elf, who goes by the name “Elaris Sel Marden,” or for short Elaris, was prized with the duty to oversee and protect the temple’s contents and ensure that no ill fate becomes the worlds that lie within. Chapter One: The Never-Ending Dunes and The Wondering Xandrixes

passages.heading: The Endless Temple - Elaris Sel Marden
passages.text:
Elaris thumbed through a series of books as he savored a bit of roast sea lizard. “Since I am enshrined in this place for eternity, I might as well come to love what I am protecting,” he mumbled with a full mouth. Elaris picked up a plain-looking book with sand on the cover and sifting out through its pages. He turned it over to find the name, but there wasn’t one. “ Well, I guess since this one doesn’t have a name, I’ll just have to read this one and find out what to call it,” he thought to himself. He decided he would leave the book on the table next to a chair and find a cup of tea to enjoy while he was reading. Elaris was trying to make the best of his situation. He had not chosen to become a scholar for the rest of his life, but things had happened that had made this his permanent occupation. He was never to leave, and he could only be replaced when he had died. A small part of him wished not to be here, but this was an honor and a much better outcome than he deserved. In the pantry, Elaris searched for what he thought to be the most suitable tea to go with his morning readings. He pushed aside one last container until he found the one he sought. It was mint herbal tea with a unique herb in it that made scholars more vividly imagine, if not envision, the book they were reading so clearly it was as if they were the narrator of the book. Now sitting in his chair and sipping his tea, he opened the book and began to read.  
		“The desert seems to extend on into eternity. Once, a great explorer named Xandri traveled further than any man had ever traveled, but he still never found the end and died in his last attempt. Not many had ever shown that kind of bravery since.” The storyteller finished and asked if there were any questions. My hand shot up almost by instinct. “What about the Xandrixes? They seem to reside in the desert without a problem. What if someone were to ride one to the end?” I questioned—the room filled with sharp gasps. The next thing I felt was a boxing to the ear.  
	My ear rang loudly, and I could feel the blood pulsing to it—one of the shamans had hit me with his cane. “We do not ride on the backs of the gods. You will be punished if we hear much more nonsense from you, Xandri.” The head shaman, Xadra, warned. I was pulled out of the crowd and taken somewhere more secluded. Another one of the shamans gave the same speech I always get. It always leads back to how I’m the son of the great explorer and should be a better example to my peers who needed someone to look up to, but I didn’t care to be the babysitter for my tribe; I wanted to explore as my father did and none of these people could stop me. I came back to reality after zoning out as I often did. The last thing I heard, and the only thing I heard, was, “I expected a better offspring from someone as great as your father.” I rolled my eyes and wondered what it must have been like to be my father. He had the same experiences I had with the tribes-people. They all held him back, keeping him from his potential until he proved himself. I had to prove myself.  
	Later that night, Xandri lay awake in his room. He stared at the ceiling and thought in silence until, finally, he had come to a resolve. He would traverse the desert and not return until he found the end. He jumped out of his bed and grabbed his pack covered in holes and bits of scant patchwork that was coming apart at the seams. His father, though significant, didn’t leave him much. They were poor, and his father’s death had left him poorer. His mother died in childbearing; he was lucky he hadn’t died with her. After packing, he walked to the mirror and cleaned himself with water from a pitcher. His skin was dark from many years under the sun and full of scales. His clan were descendants of lizards that had lived in the desert. It was said that the Xandrixes had blessed them with their human form so they may worship them and that they would turn them back to lizards if they stopped. Xandri, like his father, struggled to believe that genuinely divine creatures would be so callous. 
	As Xandri walked away from the little hut he had, he imagined that the tribe would be sorrowful with his departure, but he knew this was wishful thinking. After all, he wouldn’t be missed. He had caused more harm than good, constantly being threatened with banishment from the tribe or public flogging. That would be one thing he would never miss: all the rules. They had rules for everything, and it was stifling. Xandri pushed those thoughts to the back of his mind. It was time to focus on better things. With the sky above him and the moon lighting his way, he finally was hopeful. The moon is shown down on the dunes in a beautiful array. It was a sight to behold. The sand looked like shining sheets of silver dotted with splendid purple vines sprawled across the ground like thick webs. Small prickle bushes were scattered across the sand sea. The sight was mesmerizing. He didn’t understand why everyone feared the desert. Then he felt something. It was like a small earthquake running through the ground like a torrent wave. The sand washed forward like a crashing wave of water. He braced himself as the surge of sand swallowed him. 
	Clouds of sand blurred Xandri’s vision as he surfaced. His reptilian features helped him to traverse the desert, and things like this were not uncommon nor unprepared for. Often, great currents of wind would blow large waves of sand across the sand sea, which was the reason for the name. It was still the dead of night and getting colder as clouds washed over the night sky. He decided to sleep in the sand and use its embrace like a blanket to keep in the heat.  
	He woke to the sun beating down upon his head. He felt blistered and parched. The sun had given him a headache. He dug through his pack to find something to cover his head. He now began the journey again. The sand was torrential now. Waves washed to all corners of his vision. If he was not careful, he could be swallowed too deep to dig out and die. He realized why so many people had been afraid to traverse the desert. Of course, he knew a simple secret his father had taught: he had a boy. The sand of this particular desert moved in mysterious ways, and no one knew why, but his father knew how to use it to his advantage. Alongside the vines that snaked across the desert were large woody leaves that looked like the ears of the Zorlop. These leaves could be fashioned to one’s feet and then used to walk upon the waves without fear of getting pulled under. He then tied the leaves about his feet and began his journey again.

works.title: A Journey Into the Soul
works.blurb: an eye rendered as a whole planet, toured biome by biome down to its inner light.

passages.heading: A Journey Into the Soul
passages.text:
A Journey Into the Soul: An Expedition Into the Living Biomes of the Eye

What if the human eye wasn’t an organ, but a planet?

A Journey Into the Soul follows a lone traveler made of light — not a character, but a phenomenon — as it descends through the layered ecosystems hidden inside a single eye. The tone is clinical, dreamlike, and eerily detached, as if a research team were cataloging a world that should not exist.

This is not metaphor.  
This is fieldwork.

🌬️ The Scaly Desert of Skin

The expedition begins at the outer rim, where the skin around the eye forms a cracked, wind‑blasted desert.  
Dead skin drifts like ash.  
Dust storms rise without warning.  
The terrain feels ancient, eroded by time and blinking.

passages.heading: A Journey Into the Soul
passages.text:
Light moves across the dunes like a wandering surveyor, recording the shifting patterns of this brittle landscape.

🌊 The Milky Sea of the Sclera

Beyond the desert lies a pale, viscous ocean — the sclera reimagined as a milky sea.  
Red, sandy islands coil through the water like exposed veins.  
Strange, slow creatures drift beneath the surface, their bodies tinted the color of diluted blood.

They move with a heavy, deliberate intelligence, as if aware of the light skimming above them.

The atmosphere is cold, clinical, and unsettlingly quiet.

🌿 The Iris Forest

The iris becomes a lush, concentric rainforest.

Emerald ridges rise like terraced mountains.  
Pools of green water glow from within, casting soft halos across the foliage.  
Large worm‑like organisms slither through the undergrowth, their bodies patterned with shifting colors that mimic the iris itself.

They are primitive, but not mindless.  
They watch the light.  
They react to it.

passages.heading: A Journey Into the Soul
passages.text:
The forest feels alive in a way that suggests memory.

⬛ The Descent Into the Pupil

The pupil is not an opening.  
It is a geological event.

Smooth black cliffs plunge downward into a pit so deep it seems to erase sound.  
The descent is slow and disorienting.  
Gravity weakens.  
Pebbles drift upward.  
Dust hangs motionless in the air.

Floating islands of soft black tissue rise like embryonic moons, drifting through the void with no visible source of momentum.

Light follows them, drawn deeper into the abyss.

✨ The Soullight

At the bottom of the pupil, the darkness changes.

The faint glow from above fades.  
A new illumination rises from below — warmer, older, and impossibly steady.

This is the soul’s light.

It pulses through the floating islands, through the cliffs, through the entire biosphere.  
It reveals the eye not as a biological structure, but as a layered world built around a single radiant core.

passages.heading: A Journey Into the Soul
passages.text:
The journey ends not with revelation, but with recognition:

Every eye contains a universe.  
Every universe contains a soul.  
And light is the only witness capable of traveling between them.

works.title: A Journey Into the Heartstream: The Rite of the Blue-Born
works.blurb: a marrow-dwelling people undergo a coming-of-age rite that scatters them forever down the bloodstream.

passages.text:
A Journey Into the Heartstream: The Rite of the Blue‑Born

This chapter follows the Blue‑Born, a people who grow inside the marrow caverns of the bones. Their skin is pigmented a deep, mineral blue — the color of uncirculated blood, the color of youth before recognition.

They live in a labyrinth of glowing marrow tunnels, where the walls pulse faintly with the rhythm of the distant heart. Their society is calm, cold, and ceremonial. Everything they do prepares them for the moment they will leave the bones forever.

That moment is called The Recognition.

🦴 The Age of Recognition

When a Blue‑Born reaches adulthood, their pigment begins to fade — not to pale, but to red, the color of circulation. It is the body’s way of calling them upward.

The elders gather.  
The marrow lights dim.  
The cavern hums with the pulse of the heart.

The young men stand together, trembling not with fear but with the weight of inevitability. They have grown up side by side, carved tools together, sung marrow‑songs together, dreamed of the world above the bone.

Now they must leave it.

🚣 The Ascent to the Bloodstream

A narrow shaft opens in the bone — a vertical tunnel lined with soft, living tissue. The Blue‑Born climb, feeling the temperature rise, feeling the pulse grow louder.

At the top, they emerge into the Bloodstream.

It is not a tube.  
It is a river.

A vast, winding, crimson waterway that coils through the body like the Amazon. The current is strong. The air is humid and metallic. Strange creatures lurk beneath the surface — translucent predators shaped like cells, drifting tendrils that sting, massive immune beasts that patrol the waters.

Waiting for them is the Ceremonial Raft — a living vessel grown from tissue, shaped by tradition, guided by instinct.

They board together, still a brotherhood.

They do not know how long that will last.

🌧️ The River of Blood

The raft drifts through the bloodstream, carried by the pulse. The journey is beautiful and terrifying:

• towering artery walls rise like canyon cliffs  
• branching vessels split like river deltas  
• swirling eddies pull at the raft  
• immune creatures watch from the shadows

The young men laugh, argue, dream, and fear — all the emotions of early adulthood, amplified by the knowledge that this is the last time they will ever be together.

The river grows narrower.  
The current grows faster.  
The heart draws near.

❤️ The Heart of the Body

The heart is not a chamber.  
It is a cathedral.

A massive, thundering structure of muscle and light, beating with ancient purpose. The raft enters the atrium, and the current becomes chaotic — swirling, splitting, dividing.

The Blue‑Born try to hold onto each other, but the bloodstream does not allow it.

One by one, they are swept into different chambers, different arteries, different destinies. Their hands slip. Their voices vanish. Their faces disappear into the rushing red.

There is no time for goodbye.  
There is no ceremony for separation.  
The body simply moves them on.

This is the truth of the Heartstream:

No one stays together.  
Everyone is carried away.  
Life is a river that never lets you hold what you love for long.

works.title: The Yellow Drop and The Plain Before Sound
works.blurb: a prose poem in which falling notes of sound build a world that collapses back into waking.

passages.text:
The Yellow Drop and The Plain Before Sound

In the first morning, the ear held only a pale, waiting surface — a blank stretch of nothing that felt more like potential than space.

Then a yellow drop of sound fell.

It struck the emptiness and rippled outward in warm, trembling rings, the way the first stir of wind might ripple across a still lake. The ripple brightened the plain, hinting at depth, hinting at direction, as if the world were remembering how to begin.

A second sound followed — a high, feather‑light note that fluttered across the ripples like a bird testing the air.  
Then a deeper tone arrived, slow and weighted, settling into the ground like packed earth.  
A bright, sharp chime cracked through the space, breaking open the horizon the way a wave breaks against stone.

They fell at irregular intervals, like a hesitant composer testing notes in an empty hall.  
Each one a different shade of sound — thin silver ticks, dull red thuds, pale blue hums — spreading outward, overlapping, interfering.  
Where they crossed, new patterns formed: soft oscillations, trembling grids, invisible architecture.

This was not light painting a scene.  
This was sound building one.

High notes lifted the air, giving it height.  
Low notes thickened the ground, giving it weight.  
Mid‑tones stretched themselves into long, trembling lines that became the first hints of structure — arches of resonance, pillars of vibration, corridors made of nothing but pressure and rhythm.

The soundscape grew more intricate.  
The air thickened with tone.  
The ground hummed with quiet intention.

And still, the yellow drop kept falling.

Each drip struck the forming landscape with a steady, patient rhythm.  
Each one added a new layer of motion.  
Each one deepened the sense that something was gathering itself, preparing to become.

The rhythm quickened — not frantic, but inevitable, like a tide rising toward shore.  
The whole sound‑world leaned forward, trembling at the edge of revelation.

Then the final drop fell — bright, sharp, impossibly clear.

And the body opened its eyes.

The sound‑architecture collapsed in an instant, folding back into silence.  
The ripples flattened.  
The spires dissolved.  
The trembling ground became nothing more than sensation.

The point of view slid outward, smooth as breath — from the ear’s inner creation to the dim room beyond the eyelids.

We see now through the body’s eyes.

The alarm is buzzing.  
The morning has begun.
